本作是一款回合制塔防游戏，玩家需要管理自己的资源，为防御塔提供支持，在史莱姆的一波波冲击下保护自己的村庄。在游戏中玩家可以在每回合在“升级，改造，建造，探索”四种卡牌中使用一张来提升自己。最终通过关卡。 游戏内有着食物，木材，石头三种材料，“升级，改造，建造，探索”四种卡牌在游戏底部按顺序排放，从左到右一次为一道四星，星级越高卡牌使用时的效果越强，比如高星级的探索可以探索更多地块；改造根据一道四星可以改造普通草地，岩石，森林，麦田四种；建造根据一到四星可以建造每回合从范围内的森林中采集1木材的伐木工小屋，每回合从范围内的小麦获得2食物的农场，在范围内每个岩石匡威采集1块岩石的炸弹和在范围内攻击敌人的加农炮；升级根据星级不同提供的能力也不同，比如升级一个伐木工小屋，前三级的升级可以加大伐木工小屋的采集范围，而第四级的升级可以将伐木工小屋每回合生产的木材变为两倍。每当玩家使用一张卡牌后，这张卡牌就会被排到最左边，而其他的卡牌会依次向右移一格并升一星。如何使用卡牌，按怎样的顺序使用卡牌在本作中是很讲究策略性的。 游戏中的每个建造每回合都需要消耗食物，而且每个建造升级的卡牌都很有讲究的，比如最普通的伐木工小屋，在一开始升级获取木材双倍后，后面还可以升级根据九格范围内的木头获取木材的能力，，一回合直接18木材。 总的来说，本作虽然看起来简单，玩法也很简单，但是策略性却一点也不低，虽然只有15关战役，但是配合25种不同的建筑，6种不同的升级和20种不同的地块，是可以给玩家提供十多小时的游玩时长的，推荐喜欢塔防的玩家游玩。 [quote]欢迎关注鉴赏家: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/DCYXJLB] 大川游戏俱乐部 [/url] 欢迎加入Steam组:[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45300930] 大川游戏俱乐部 [/url] 来一起感受游戏的乐趣喜欢这篇评论，也是可以顺手点个赞哟[/quote]

I don't like to review games unless I get very far into them or beat them, but I don't know if I will ever get far enough in this game to do so, so I'll just leave a review now. I'm rating this positively but I do have some concerns. Let me explain. The game is looks fine, animates well, is entertaining in many ways, and carries relatively a high production value. I like that it works well with controller and M&K and is steam deck ready. It's a pretty challenging game and it appears to have a lot of levels and objectives, so the value is definitely there. My problem is that it's not that fun. It's kind of a tower defense game but you also have to manage an economy. But you're not given the freedom that you think you'd get in a game like this. Every round gives you one thing to do. So you can't build towers every round. You'll also have to manage your resources and if you go dry, your towers won't even fire. I was more frustrated and bothered by these mechanics. And it's a shame because the game looks like it could be fun. Ultimately, it's more of a puzzle turn-based game than a traditional tower defense game. In fact, it seems that to progress and get all the optional objectives, you'll have to play a certain way. I hate that. I can't in good conscience give this a thumbs down because it is a good game. I just wish it wasn't so constraining with it's gameplay elements.

Islets Defense is one of those rare strategy games that manages to feel both familiar and genuinely fresh at the same time. Developed by MiniGoof and published by Nuntius Games, MiniGoof, and Vsoo Games, it takes the well-worn foundations of tower defense and reshapes them into something slower, more deliberate, and far more thoughtful. Instead of testing your reflexes and multitasking under pressure, it challenges your ability to plan, sequence, and optimize decisions over time. The result is a hybrid experience that sits somewhere between tower defense, puzzle design, and board game strategy. The most defining aspect of the game is its turn-based structure. Every action you take—whether building a structure, upgrading defenses, exploring new tiles, or modifying terrain—counts as a turn, and enemy waves advance in response to your decisions. This fundamentally changes how the game feels. Rather than reacting in real time, you’re constantly weighing trade-offs: do you invest in long-term resource generation, or prepare immediately for the next threat? Do you expand your map for future opportunities, or consolidate what you already have? This constant tension between short-term survival and long-term efficiency gives the game a strategic weight that most tower defense titles don’t attempt. What elevates this system further is the action queue mechanic. Your available actions rotate in a sequence, and their effectiveness depends on their position—actions become stronger the longer you wait to use them. This introduces a layer of timing and sequencing that goes beyond simple decision-making. You’re not just choosing what to do, but also when to do it for maximum impact. This creates a satisfying rhythm of planning ahead, holding back, and then executing stronger moves at the right moment. It transforms what could have been a static system into something dynamic and engaging, rewarding foresight and efficiency. The game also expands beyond traditional tower placement by incorporating resource management and exploration. You’re not just defending a path—you’re building a small, functional settlement. Resources like food, wood, and stone are required to sustain and upgrade your defenses, and the map begins partially hidden, encouraging you to explore and uncover new tiles. This adds a sense of progression that feels organic, as each decision contributes not only to your immediate survival but also to the long-term strength of your setup. The interplay between exploration and defense keeps the gameplay loop from becoming too narrow, giving each run a slightly different flow depending on how you expand. Content variety helps reinforce this structure. The game features multiple stages and biomes, each introducing new modifiers, layouts, and challenges that force you to rethink your approach. Some maps emphasize resource scarcity, others introduce unique environmental interactions, and later stages demand tighter optimization and more precise planning. This ensures that the core mechanics are tested in different ways, preventing the experience from becoming too predictable too quickly. At its best, each level feels like a self-contained puzzle, asking you to understand its rules and solve it as efficiently as possible. Visually, Islets Defense adopts a clean and colorful style that complements its design philosophy. The presentation is bright and readable, with clear distinctions between tiles, structures, and enemies. This clarity is essential for a game built around planning, as it allows you to quickly assess the board and make informed decisions. The overall aesthetic leans toward a light, almost cozy tone, which contrasts nicely with the depth of its systems. It’s inviting without being distracting, and it reinforces the idea that this is a game about thinking rather than reacting. Despite its strengths, the game is not without its limitations. The turn-based pacing, while innovative, can feel slow for players accustomed to the immediacy of traditional tower defense. The deliberate nature of each action means that the game lacks the adrenaline-driven moments that define the genre for many players. Additionally, the handcrafted nature of its maps means that replayability is tied more to optimization than discovery. Once you understand a level, it becomes possible to approach it with a fixed strategy, which can reduce long-term variety. There is also a sense that the game’s systems, while strong, are not fully pushed to their limits. The mechanics remain consistent throughout, and while new modifiers and layouts introduce variation, the core loop does not evolve dramatically. For some players, this consistency is a strength, providing a stable and learnable system. For others, it may feel like the game stops just short of reaching its full potential, especially after mastering its fundamentals. Even so, Islets Defense succeeds because it understands what it wants to be and executes it with clarity. It transforms tower defense into a more thoughtful, strategic experience, one that rewards patience, planning, and efficiency over speed and reflexes. It is a game that invites you to slow down, consider your options, and find satisfaction in optimizing your approach rather than simply surviving. For players who enjoy puzzle-like strategy games and are drawn to systems that reward careful planning, it offers a distinctive and engaging experience that stands out within its genre. For those seeking fast-paced action or constant mechanical evolution, it may feel too restrained to fully satisfy. It is a focused, well-crafted game that doesn’t try to be everything—but within its chosen space, it delivers something genuinely refreshing. Rating: 8/10

Fun little puzzley build-order-focused tower defense game. You have four different base buildings and can get various upgraded towers and buildings via chests/shops. Starts pretty basic and easy but ramps up nicely. Took me about 7 hours to get perfects on the base game (15 maps) and there are hardcore versions after that, which are more difficult. You will have to restart some maps because there's no undo or save, but maps generally top out at 30 min a pop so it's not super onerous. Not going to knock your socks off, but it does everything well with no bugs and a pleasing presentation. 8/10 edit after 100%: took another 10 hours to do the hardcore versions, some of which are quite tricky. If you're the type that likes a build order puzzle, this one will certainly scratch the itch. It's nicely refined and well worth a look.

This game has exceeded my expectations! It's been a long time since I've played a tower defense game, and I figured I may as well try it since I got it as a mystery key online. I have so far finished the first three biomes and it's crazy fun, the way it manages to keep things fresh with biome-specific gimmicks, random minigames and traps for the player made me appreciate how well the developers managed to entertain the player through this tried and tested game format with a great spin. I also enjoy the turn-based, resource management aspect of it as it makes you think how to balance things out, and while I haven't much tried to take part in the leaderboard or hardcore mode, they seem like great ways to boost replayability and you just can't help but start to wonder how you could beat your PB, which is great. Criminally underrated, I'd encourage anyone to give it a try!

I won this game through SteamGifts. Islets Defense was a really pleasant surprise for me. The graphics are lovely, the gameplay feels polished, and the mechanics stay interesting because the game keeps introducing little twists and new ideas as you progress. I had a lot of fun with it overall. That said, the difficulty curve gave me a bit of whiplash. Early on it felt very forgiving, like you could kind of do whatever and still win, but later some levels became super punishing where one small mistake basically meant restarting the whole thing. I got pretty close to giving up a few times, honestly. I didn’t even touch hardcore mode because normal mode was already destroying me enough. I’d also say the “tower defense” label is a bit misleading. It feels more like a turn-based strategy game since you can only do one action per turn and can’t freely spam buildings whenever you want. Not a bad thing at all, just different from what I expected going in. Even with the difficulty headaches and the lack of strategy guides online when I got stuck, I still think it’s a genuinely good game and definitely worth recommending if you enjoy strategy games that make you think a bit.

（重要的事：如果你进不去游戏记得更新显卡驱动）这与其说是个塔防游戏，倒不如说是个资源收集游戏。如果你只喜欢玩传统塔防，喜欢丰富的防御塔和敌人，那这个作品估计很难对您口味了。这个游戏的核心玩法是规划和运营，很多情况下塔和敌人只有一种，你需要不断收集资源升级防御塔，同时还要兼顾资源的平衡和地图探索。关卡设计上前三章都是比较轻松愉快且有趣的，将游戏玩法运用的很好，但是在这之后游戏就开始上难度了。总之这是一款侧重于资源收集和地图探索的塔防游戏，回合制的形式让人有更多的思考空间。建造，升级，改造，探索的卡组循环与牌序调整也为这个游戏增添了卡牌游戏的策略感。总之这是一个偏静态和思考的游戏。 （Important: If you can’t get into the game, remember to update your graphics driver!）This isn’t really a tower defense game; it’s more of a resource-collecting adventure. If you’re looking for traditional tower defense with tons of rich defenses and enemies, you’ll probably find this game too limiting for your tastes. The core gameplay is about planning and managing your resources. In many cases, there’s only one type of tower and one type of enemy—you need to constantly collect resources to upgrade your defenses while balancing everything and exploring the map. The first three chapters are pretty relaxing, fun, and well-executed, but after that the difficulty ramps up. Overall, this is a tower defense game focused on resource collection and map exploration. The turn-based format gives you plenty of room to think. The building, upgrading, transforming, and exploring card cycles, along with adjusting card order, add a strategic deck-building feel. In short, it’s a more static and thoughtful game.
